name: Barberry (Berberis vulgaris)
short: A toxicology review of barberry and its constituent berberine lists gut upset, jaundice and heart and nerve toxicity as dose dependent, and urges caution in pregnancy, newborns and G6PD deficiency.
text: Most of the evidence concerns barberry together with berberine, its main alkaloid, rather than barberry alone. A toxicology review covering both says there are reports of negative effects in animals and humans and that, depending on dose, route and duration, they could cause gastrointestinal upset and ulceration, immunotoxicity, phototoxicity, neurotoxicity, cardiotoxicity and jaundice; it advises caution in pregnancy, in newborns and in people with G6PD deficiency. The abstract does not say which of these effects were seen in people and which only in animal or laboratory studies. A meta-analysis of five randomised trials of barberry itself (339 participants) calls barberry a safe approach in its title, but its abstract reports no adverse-event data. On the other side, a clinical review that drew on 77 human studies of barberry and berberine states, about berberine, that it has very low toxicity in usual doses, without major side effects, and that only mild gastrointestinal reactions may occur in some patients. For interactions, the toxicology review advises care when berberine is taken with drugs metabolised by CYP enzymes, and a review of cytochrome P450 studies says berberine's inhibition of CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 is its most important potential drug interaction and that barberry's effect on multiple CYP450 enzymes calls for clinical checks, while noting that clinical trials are still needed; neither abstract names individual medicines.
